Course Catalog Description

This seminar is an introduction to some dimension of the history of a nation, region, people, culture, institution, or historical phenomenon selected by the respective instructor. Students will come to understand, and develop an appreciation for: the origins and evolution of the people, cultures, and/or political, economic, and/or social institutions of a particular region(s) of the world. They may explore how human encounters shaped individual and collective identities and the political, economic, and social orders of the region/nation/communities under study. Instructors prioritize critical reading, engaged participation, and focused writing assignments.

Class Description

Enslavement—not least because of the horrendous statistics on global human trafficking—remains an enduring phenomenon and a topic of central interest to historians. The extent and nature of involuntary servitude today is difficult to measure, because since Mauretania abolished slavery in 1981 (but a law prosecuting slaveholders passed only in 2007 and has been sporadically enforced) it is no longer legal anywhere. In contrast, involuntary servitude, or slavery, was entirely legal in the Roman empire. Ancient sources, both in Latin and Greek, the principal languages of the Roman empire, tell us a great deal about enslaved persons, but nearly exclusively from the perspective of the masters and owners. Further, it is very difficult to quantify slavery, to gain a sense of the proportion of enslaved persons in the labor force, their origin, or their percentage at different points in time. In part, this is due to the vast expanse of the Roman empire, with many regional differences, which included different forms of agricultural and other labor, different levels of urbanization, and so on. The assessment and characterization of slavery and its role in the Roman empire depends, perhaps more than with any other topic, on a scholar’s methods and assumptions, specifically, what they think about the Roman economy. Therefore, in this course we will read mostly ancient sources (in translation) that describe various aspects of slavery, but also some contemporary scholarly debates about enslavement in Rome based on different economic theories.
